Nice — great area to explore. Below are nearby places and experiences you can easily combine with a visit to Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit/Medora) — short descriptions and approximate distances/time from Medora where helpful.

Top picks
- Medora (town) — gateway to the park with wooden sidewalks, shops, restaurants, and several small museums (Chateau de Mores State Historic Site, North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame). The town itself is worth an hour or two. ([discovermedora.com](https://discovermedora.com/?utm_source=openai))

- Burning Hills Amphitheatre & the Medora Musical — outdoor evening musical/theatrical show in summer (seasonal); a classic Badlands experience if it’s running while you’re there. ([medorand.org](https://medorand.org/things-to-do?utm_source=openai))

- Bully Pulpit Golf Course — scenic course just outside Medora for a unique “Badlands” round. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/cities/medora?utm_source=openai))

- Chateau de Mores State Historic Site — historic house museum about early settlement and the Marquis de Mores; right near Medora. Good for 30–60 minutes. ([history.nd.gov](https://www.history.nd.gov/historicsites/chateau/?utm_source=openai))

- Maah Daah Hey Trail & mountain‑biking/hiking opportunities — extensive singletrack trail system that links areas near the park; great for day hikes, mountain biking (off‑park sections), and backcountry access. Several trailheads are reachable from Medora. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maah_Daah_Hey_Trail?utm_source=openai))

Key park/landscape spots (if you haven’t already seen them)
- Painted Canyon Overlook / Visitor Center — dramatic Badlands overlooks visible right off I‑94; an easy stop if you’re coming from the east or west. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/best-places/8-things-see-and-do-theodore-roosevelt-national-park?utm_source=openai))

- Elkhorn Ranch site (part of the park) — the remote site of TR’s ranch; more rugged access but historically interesting. The Elkhorn unit is reached by gravel roads north of Medora. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/national-park/elkhorn-ranch?utm_source=openai))

Nearby drives & day trips
- North Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park — a very different landscape and overlooks; the North Unit is roughly 65–75 miles north of Medora (plan 1.5–2+ hours driving one way). If you have time, it’s worth the drive. ([npgallery.nps.gov](https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/257b1284-d776-43d5-9a8f-863023a2e520/original.pdf?utm_source=openai))

- Enchanted Highway (Regent/Gladstone sculptures) — giant scrap‑metal sculptures along a scenic local road; roughly a 45–50 mile drive from Medora to the northern end/start of the highway and a nice half‑day diversion. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/itineraries/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))

- Little Missouri National Grassland / gravel scenic byways — exploratory gravel roads, prairie views and quiet badlands outside the park; good if you like low‑traffic scenic drives and photography. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/scenic-drives?utm_source=openai))

Practical notes
- Dickinson (about 35 miles east) is the nearest larger town for groceries, restaurants, lodging, and medical services. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Road/seasonal: some park roads, overlooks, and seasonal activities (like the Medora Musical) are weather/season dependent — check current park and Medora event pages if you want to confirm hours or closures. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))

Great question — Medora is small but packed with classic Badlands experiences. Here are the best things to do, with quick notes and tips so you can plan:

Top things to do
- Explore Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit): drive the 36-mile Scenic Loop from the Medora visitor center, stop at Painted Canyon and Boicourt/Medora overlooks, and hike short trails (Wind Canyon, Skyline Vista) for badlands views and wildlife (bison, prairie dogs, wild horses). Check park alerts/fees before you go. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))

- See the Medora Musical at the Burning Hills Amphitheatre: the long-running summer outdoor show is a signature Medora experience — often paired with the Tjaden Terrace/terrace events. Buy tickets from the official site/ticket office. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/?utm_source=openai))

- Do the Pitchfork Steak Fondue (dinner with a view): the pitchfork-steak “fondue” dinner next to the amphitheatre is a Medora tradition and popular option for dinner + show nights. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/2022-DIGITAL-In-Town-Guide.pdf?utm_source=openai))

- Visit the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library: the new TR Presidential Library opened in 2026 near Medora and is now a major museum attraction about Roosevelt’s life and ties to the Badlands. Check its hours and any special exhibits. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/?utm_source=openai))

- Chateau de Mores State Historic Site and town walking tours: tour the 1880s chateau/interpretive center and use Medora’s self-guided or ranger-led historic walks to learn about the Marquis de Mores and early town history. ([history.nd.gov](https://www.history.nd.gov/historicsites/chateau/?utm_source=openai))

- North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame & Harold Schafer Heritage/interpretive spots: great for western/history exhibits and quick indoor options if the weather turns. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/cowboyhalloffame/?utm_source=openai))

- Rough Rider State Park + Maah Daah Hey Trail: access excellent mountain‑biking, hiking and horseback riding (Maah Daah Hey Trail trailheads are near Medora); Rough Rider (formerly Sully Creek) is the local state‑park base/campground. ([parkrec.nd.gov](https://www.parkrec.nd.gov/rough-rider-state-park?utm_source=openai))

- Bully Pulpit Golf Course: a scenic course set in the Badlands a few miles from town — memorable if you play golf. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/medora/attractions-entertainment/landmark-attractions/bully-pulpit-golf-course?utm_source=openai))

- Family / town activities: Point to Point Park (mini‑golf, lazy river/splash pad, zipline), town square shows and the Old Town Hall Theater (magic, Roosevelt presentations, folk shows) make Medora fun for kids and non‑hikers. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/2023-In-Town-Guide.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Practical tips
- Best time: summer (mid‑June through early September) for the Medora Musical, town programming and Pitchfork Fondue; the park is open year‑round but weather/winter road conditions matter. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/?utm_source=openai))  
- Wildlife viewing: early morning or evening increases chances to see bison and wildlife in TRNP. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/hiking-in-the-south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Book ahead: musical tickets, the Pitchfork Fondue, tee times at Bully Pulpit, and popular guided rides/tours can sell out in summer — use official sites (medora.com, trlibrary.com, nps.gov). ([medora.com](https://medora.com/?utm_source=openai))  
- Essentials: bring water, sunscreen, layers (Badlands weather changes quickly), and a camera/binoculars for wildlife and vistas. Check NPS alerts before trail/road plans. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/visitorcenters.htm/index.htm?utm_source=openai))

Quick sample plans
- Half‑day (if you’re short on time): Painted Canyon overlook + short South Unit scenic‑drive highlights (Wind Canyon/Boicourt) and a walk in Medora town square. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/best-places/8-things-see-and-do-theodore-roosevelt-national-park?utm_source=openai))  
- Full day: South Unit scenic loop with hikes + lunch in Medora, afternoon at Chateau de Mores or the Cowboy Hall of Fame, evening Medora Musical + Pitchfork Fondue. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/hiking-in-the-south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Two+ days: add Maah Daah Hey riding/hiking or mountain biking from Rough Rider State Park and a round at Bully Pulpit. ([parkrec.nd.gov](https://www.parkrec.nd.gov/rough-rider-state-park?utm_source=openai))

Great — here’s a compact, driveable 3-day road-trip through western North Dakota with the must-see stops, estimated drive times, and activity suggestions. If you’ll tell me your starting town (Bismarck, Fargo, Dickinson, or elsewhere), travel dates, and whether you prefer hiking/camping or short walks and museums, I’ll tailor this to you.

Overview (loopable, ~300–500 miles total depending on exact route)
- Focus: Dickinson → Medora / Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit) → Watford City / TRNP (North Unit) → Williston / Fort Union → optional Enchanted Highway / Regent.  
- Highlights: Theodore Roosevelt National Park (both units), Medora (historic town & Chateau de Mores), Enchanted Highway (giant metal sculptures), Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson), Fort Union Trading Post NHS (Williston area). ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/things2do.htm?utm_source=openai))

Day 1 — Dickinson to Medora (Badlands + Old West)
- Morning: Start in Dickinson — visit the Dickinson Museum Center / Badlands Dinosaur Museum (excellent regional dinosaur/fossil displays and Prairie Outpost Park). Plan 1–2 hours. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/dickinson/attractions-entertainment/educational-attractions/dickinson-museum-center?utm_source=openai))
- Midday: Drive west to Medora (about 30–45 minutes from Dickinson). Explore Medora’s Old West downtown, Chateau de Mores, and short walks. If your timing is right, take the 36–48 mile scenic loop through the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park (visitor center/overlooks and likely wildlife viewing). Allow 3–4 hours for the park loop, hikes or overlooks. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/things2do.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Evening: Stay overnight in Medora (several small hotels/B&Bs/cabins). In summer, consider the Medora Musical or evening walking tours (seasonal).

Day 2 — Medora / TRNP South Unit then north toward Watford City (North Unit)
- Morning: Return to any South Unit overlooks or do a short hike (Coal Vein Trail, Buck Hill, or Boicourt). The South Unit Visitor Center near Medora has park info and exhibits. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/visitorcenters.htm/index.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Midday: Drive north toward Watford City (expect ~1.5–2 hours depending on stops and exact route). Use the Maah Daah Hey access points or Little Missouri National Grassland pullouts if you want short backcountry hikes or prairie-dog towns. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/best-places/8-things-see-and-do-theodore-roosevelt-national-park?utm_source=openai))
- Afternoon/Evening: Explore the North Unit (scenic byway, Oxbow Overlook, prairie-dog towns, bison sightings). Watford City is the nearest town for lodging and dining. Overnight in Watford City. ([visitwatfordcity.com](https://www.visitwatfordcity.com/Discover?utm_source=openai))

Day 3 — Watford City to Williston (Fort Union) or loop back via the Enchanted Highway
Option A — Northward (history + river scenery)
- Morning: Head from Watford City to Williston (roughly ~45–60 minutes / ~45 miles). Visit Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site (reconstructed fur-trade fort on the Montana/North Dakota border) and nearby Missouri River overlooks. Great spot for history and river scenery. ([travelmath.com](https://www.travelmath.com/cities-on-the-way/from/Watford%2BCity%2C%2BND/to/Williston%2C%2BND?utm_source=openai))
- Afternoon: If time allows, explore Lake Sakakawea viewpoints / drive along Highway 1804, then return toward Dickinson/Medora or continue on toward Montana.

Option B — Southerly loop (quirky art + small towns)
- Drive back toward I‑94, then east to the Enchanted Highway (starts at I‑94 Exit 72 near Gladstone and runs ~32 miles south to Regent). Stop at each large metal sculpture (photo ops, picnic shelters, small gift shop in Regent). From Regent you can loop back to Dickinson. Expect this detour to add 1–2 hours of driving plus time at the sculptures. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/itineraries/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))

Practical tips
- Fuel & services: Distances between towns can be long; fill up in Dickinson, Medora, Watford City, or Williston. Cell service is spotty in some badlands and grassland areas.  
- Wildlife & safety: Best wildlife viewing is early morning or late afternoon in TRNP. Use pullouts; stay in your vehicle for close encounters and follow park rules. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/things2do.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Seasonal notes: Some attractions (Medora Musical, visitor-center hours, museum hours) are seasonal — check schedules before you go. Roads in remote areas may be gravel; a vehicle with decent clearance helps for side roads. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/2026-In-Town-Guide-Digital.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Time budget: Each “must” stop usually needs 45–180 minutes (short overlooks vs museum/park loops). For a relaxed 3-day trip, plan 3–5 main stops per day including meals and drives.

- Build the itinerary into a turn-by-turn day plan with exact distances and estimated drive times from your specific start town.  
- Give lodging/campsite recommendations (Medora, Watford City, Williston, Dickinson) and link to current hours/tickets for Medora Musical or TRNP visitor centers.

Nice route — you’ll cross from the Black Hills into true badlands and prairie scenery. Below are stops I recommend (in the order you’d hit them on a typical drive from Mount Rushmore/Keystone toward Medora / the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt NP), with short notes on why each is worth it and how much time to allow.

Quick baseline
- Mount Rushmore → Medora (Medora is the town at the South Unit entrance): roughly 4–5 hours of driving; about 260–290 miles depending on route. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/a-map-to-medora/?utm_source=openai))

Suggested stops (order + why + time)
1. Custer State Park & Needles Highway (via US‑16A / Iron Mountain Road) — if you haven’t already done it, this scenic loop (granite spires, tunnels, wildlife loop for bison) is an iconic Black Hills detour and pairs well with Mount Rushmore. 1–3 hours for a short drive and a lookout/hike. ([blackhillsvacations.com](https://www.blackhillsvacations.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/BHCR21_Map_MtRushmore_FNL.pdf?utm_source=openai))

2. Crazy Horse Memorial (nearby) — large cultural/art project and visitor center; quick stop for photos and the story behind the monument. 30–60 minutes.

3. Badlands National Park (Ben Reifel/Badlands Loop Road, overlooks and short trails like Notch or Fossil Exhibit) — lunar-looking eroded formations, great for sunrise/sunset photos and quick hikes. Plan 1–3 hours for the Loop Road + a short trail; longer if you want hikes. (Badlands is a natural, obvious stop between the Black Hills and Medora). ([travelmath.com](https://www.travelmath.com/distance/from/Mount%2BRushmore/to/Badlands%2BNational%2BPark?utm_source=openai))

4. Wall / Wall Drug — classic kitschy roadside stop: coffee deals, shops, photo ops, a fun place to stretch legs and eat. Good for families and a classic South Dakota experience. 30–60 minutes. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Drug?utm_source=openai))

5. Minuteman Missile National Historic Site (Delta‑01/Delta‑09 visitor centers near I‑90 exits east of Wall) — short but striking Cold War history stop; interpretive center and a preserved launch control/​silo site (book in advance if you want a silo tour). 45–90 minutes. ([wall-badlands.com](https://www.wall-badlands.com/things-to-do/attractions/?utm_source=openai))

6. Prairie Homestead (historic sod house) — a quick, evocative historic site near the Badlands/I‑90 corridor showing settler life; useful stop if you like small historic sites. 20–40 minutes. ([assets.simpleviewinc.com](https://assets.simpleviewinc.com/simpleview/image/upload/v1/clients/blackhillsbadlandssd/2026AttractionMap_Digital_ad9ef7db-38c6-4ff4-b90a-8a66fbafe219.pdf?utm_source=openai))

7. (Optional detour) Devil’s Tower, WY — if you want a major geological monument and don’t mind ~1.5–2 hour detour northwest from the Black Hills/Belle Fourche area, this is a great add-on.

8. En route north to Medora: take US‑85 north (the Theodore Roosevelt Expressway) into western North Dakota — a scenic high‑plains drive that brings you directly toward Medora and the South Unit. The Medora area and Painted Canyon overlooks are excellent lead‑ins to the park. The South Unit’s scenic loop drive itself is ~48 miles and usually takes about 2 hours without stops (but allow extra time for wildlife/viewpoints). ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/itineraries/sturgis-medora?utm_source=openai))

Final destination — Medora / Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
- Plan time to drive the South Unit scenic loop, walk some short trails, and visit the Painted Canyon Visitor Center or the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in town. Fuel, food, and lodging are concentrated in Medora/Dickinson — top up before you head into park roads. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/things2do.htm?utm_source=openai))

Practical tips
- Time and fuel: many long stretches have limited services — keep your tank topped and carry water/snacks. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/faq/getting-here?utm_source=openai))
- Cell coverage can be spotty through the badlands/grasslands; download maps ahead of time. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/faq/getting-here?utm_source=openai))
- Check seasonal/road conditions: Badlands and TRNP road status and opening times can change with weather; look up NPS alerts the day of travel. ([travelmath.com](https://www.travelmath.com/distance/from/Mount%2BRushmore/to/Badlands%2BNational%2BPark?utm_source=openai))
- Silo/structured tours (Minuteman Missile) can require reservations; check ahead. ([npshistory.com](https://www.npshistory.com/publications/badl/brochures/visitor-info.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Time zones: western North Dakota/Medora is Mountain Time (you may cross time zones depending on your route), so watch your watch/phone. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/directions?utm_source=openai))

Nice question — I-94 across North Dakota has a surprising number of great (and quirky) stops. Below are the best picks, listed west→east with a short note on why each is worth a pull‑off and an approximate exit or location.

- Painted Canyon overlook / Medora & Theodore Roosevelt National Park (south unit) — dramatic Badlands views, short hikes, wildlife (bison/pronghorn, prairie dogs) and the Medora town/entertainment (Medora Musical, cowboy history). Very easy to add a 1–3 hour visit. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/best-places/8-things-see-and-do-theodore-roosevelt-national-park?utm_source=openai))

- Enchanted Highway (Gladstone → Regent) — a 32‑mile series of gigantic scrap‑metal sculptures (start at I‑94 Exit 72); unique photo ops and small attractions in Regent. Plan 1–3 hours (or a half‑day if you want every sculpture). ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/regent/attractions-entertainment/family-fun/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))

- Beach / Prairie Fire Pottery — a short, artsy detour just off I‑94 for handmade North Dakota pottery and a pleasant small‑town stop near the western Badlands. Good for a quick break or souvenir. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/beach/attractions-entertainment/arts-attractions/prairie-fire-pottery?utm_source=openai))

- Dickinson / Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson Museum Center) — one of the state’s best family stops with full‑scale dinosaur displays and regional history; a solid 1–2 hour museum stop. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/dickinson/attractions-entertainment/educational-attractions/dickinson-museum-center?utm_source=openai))

- Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park & Mandan/Bismarck area — reconstructed On‑A‑Slant Mandan village, Custer House, Missouri River bluffs; combine with the North Dakota State Capitol area and North Dakota Heritage Center (excellent state museum and paleontology exhibits). Allow 2–3+ hours. ([mystateparks.com](https://www.mystateparks.com/parks/nd-fort-abraham-lincoln-state-park?utm_source=openai))

Here’s a concise summary of Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt’s (1858–1919) major accomplishments, his conservation work, and his lasting legacy.

Major accomplishments
- Became the youngest U.S. president (age 42) after William McKinley’s assassination and served 1901–1909.  
- Domestic policy / Progressive reforms (the “Square Deal”): used federal power to regulate big business, protect consumers, and mediate labor disputes.  
  - Trust-busting: prosecuted major monopolies (e.g., Northern Securities) and enforced antitrust laws to break or rein in corporate combinations.  
  - Consumer protection: pushed and signed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act (both 1906).  
  - Regulatory reform: strengthened the Interstate Commerce Commission through the Hepburn Act (1906) to regulate railroads.  
  - Labor: intervened in the 1902 anthracite coal strike, threatening federal takeover and forcing arbitration — an important precedent for federal mediation.  
- Foreign policy and national power: advanced “Big Stick” diplomacy, built up the U.S. Navy (including sending the Great White Fleet on a world cruise, 1907–1909), and greatly increased American influence overseas.  
- Panama Canal: orchestrated U.S. effort to secure rights to build the Panama Canal (support for Panamanian independence and the 1903 treaty granting canal rights), a strategic achievement whose construction was completed after his presidency (1914).  
- Peacemaker: mediated the end of the Russo–Japanese War and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906.  
- Political leadership beyond the White House: championed progressive ideas (later articulated as “New Nationalism”) and ran as the Progressive (“Bull Moose”) Party candidate in 1912, which reshaped early 20th‑century American politics.

Conservation work
- Philosophy and priority: made conservation a central national priority, arguing that natural resources must be managed scientifically and preserved for public use.  
- Institutional achievements: created and expanded federal conservation institutions — appointed Gifford Pinchot as the first head of the U.S. Forest Service (1905) and promoted professional, scientific management of forests and water resources.  
- Land protection and law: used new and existing authorities (including the Antiquities Act of 1906) to protect large tracts of land — establishing national forests (forest reserves), wildlife refuges (bird reservations), national parks and national monuments.  
- Scale: during his administration he set aside on the order of hundreds of millions of acres of public land for conservation (national forests, bird reserves, monuments, etc.), greatly expanding the federal role in land protection.  
- Reclamation and western development: supported the Newlands Reclamation Act (1902) to fund irrigation and reclamation projects in the arid West, tying conservation to responsible development.

Legacy — lasting impacts and controversies
- Lasting impacts:
  - Modern presidency: transformed the office into an active, agenda‑setting national leadership role and expanded executive power and use of federal authority to solve social and economic problems.  
  - Progressive policy foundations: his antitrust enforcement, consumer‑protection laws, and regulatory reforms helped establish the regulatory state and Progressive Era reforms that continued under later presidents.  
  - Conservation movement: widely regarded as the founder of the modern American conservation movement; many of today’s national parks, forests, and conservation institutions trace roots to his policies.  
  - Global stature: advanced the United States as an active world power with global interests and responsibilities.  
- Controversies and criticisms:
  - Imperialism and interventionism: his actions in Panama and his Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1904) justified frequent U.S. intervention in Latin America — criticized as imperialist and paternalistic.  
  - Race and domestic policy: complex record — he invited Booker T. Washington to the White House (1901), but his broader record includes policies and attitudes that fall short of modern standards on race and equality.  
  - Political consequences: his 1912 third‑party run split the Republican vote and helped elect Woodrow Wilson, an outcome critics view as politically harmful.  
- Cultural legacy: an enduring American icon — Rough Rider hero image, “big stick” aphorism, the “man in the arena” ethos — and one of the four presidents carved on Mount Rushmore. His name and ideas influenced later reformers and presidents (including his distant cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt in some policy areas).

Bottom line
Roosevelt remade the presidency and the federal government’s role in the economy and natural‑resource management. He combined progressive domestic reform and aggressive internationalism with a pioneering conservation program that permanently reshaped how the U.S. treats public lands — a record that is admired for its vision and criticized for its imperialist and sometimes paternalistic excesses.

Short answer: Theodore Roosevelt’s Square Deal was his domestic program (as president 1901–1909) aimed at ensuring fairness for ordinary Americans by rebalancing power among big business, labor, consumers, and the public interest. Roosevelt summarized it with the “three Cs”: control of corporations, consumer protection, and conservation of natural resources.

Key goals
- Control abusive corporate power so large trusts and monopolies couldn’t exploit consumers or crush competition.  
- Protect consumers by improving food and drug safety and creating regulatory standards.  
- Conserve natural resources and manage public lands for the long term.  
- Mediate labor disputes and promote fair treatment of workers.  

Major methods and examples
- Trust regulation and antitrust action: Roosevelt distinguished “good” trusts (to be regulated) from “bad” trusts (to be broken). His administration brought high-profile antitrust suits (for example against Northern Securities) and used the Sherman Antitrust Act to limit corporate abuses.  
- Regulation of commerce: laws and agencies strengthened federal oversight of railroads and other industries (for example the Elkins and Hepburn-era reforms expanded federal regulatory reach).  
- Consumer-protection laws: the administration pushed for and helped secure the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act (1906), raising safety and labeling standards.  
- Labor intervention: Roosevelt used the presidency as an impartial arbiter in disputes when necessary—most famously in the 1902 anthracite coal strike, where he pressured both sides to negotiate and helped secure a compromise favorable to public needs and miners’ interests.  
- Conservation initiatives: he greatly expanded the national forest system, created wildlife refuges and national monuments, and promoted federal management of water and land (including support for western reclamation projects) to preserve resources for future use.

Why it mattered
- The Square Deal marked a significant expansion of federal authority in economic and social policy and helped define the Progressive Era’s goals: curb concentrated economic power, protect ordinary consumers and workers, and steward natural resources. It set precedents for later regulatory and welfare reforms.

The four presidents carved on Mount Rushmore are, left to right: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln.

Why Theodore Roosevelt was included
- The sculptor Gutzon Borglum chose the four men to represent key themes in U.S. history: Washington (birth), Jefferson (expansion), Roosevelt (development), and Lincoln (preservation).

- Borglum and the project’s backers felt Roosevelt’s energetic, reforming image fit the monument’s narrative of national growth and vitality.

Short answer
- The Roosevelt Corollary (1904) was President Theodore Roosevelt’s addition to the Monroe Doctrine that declared the United States had the right to act as an “international police power” in the Western Hemisphere to prevent European intervention. In practice it justified U.S. intervention in Latin American countries to protect stability and U.S. interests.

What it said and where it came from
- Monroe Doctrine (Dec. 2, 1823): originally warned European powers against new colonization or intervention in the Americas. It was principally a warning to Europe, not a license for U.S. intervention in its neighbors’ internal affairs.
- Roosevelt Corollary (Dec. 1904): Roosevelt argued that if a Latin American state engaged in “chronic wrongdoing” or defaulted on debts so that European powers might intervene, the United States would step in first to restore order and collect debts — thereby preventing European military intervention. This grew out of concerns about European debt-collection efforts (e.g., in the Dominican Republic) and Roosevelt’s “big stick” foreign-policy outlook.

How it was applied (examples)
- The Corollary was used to justify many early-20th-century U.S. actions in the hemisphere: interventions, occupations, and financial control in places such as the Dominican Republic (U.S. financial control and later occupation), Nicaragua, Haiti (1915–1934), and others. It complemented earlier measures like the Platt Amendment (Cuba, 1901) and underpinned U.S. involvement around the Panama Canal.

Why it matters
- Established U.S. regional hegemony: It turned the Monroe Doctrine from a defensive warning to a basis for active U.S. policing in the Americas.
- Legal/political precedent: It provided a diplomatic and moral rationale for unilateral intervention, military occupation, and control of finances in sovereign states.
- Long-term consequences for relations: It fostered resentment and anti‑American sentiment across Latin America and shaped a legacy of distrust toward U.S. policy in the region.
- Influenced later policy shifts: The Corollary’s interventionist logic dominated U.S. policy into the 1920s and 1930s and was formally repudiated as a guiding principle by Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Good Neighbor Policy (starting 1933–34), which emphasized nonintervention and cooperation.
- Ongoing relevance: Historians, policymakers, and activists still refer to the Corollary when discussing U.S. interventionism, hemispheric security policy, and debates over sovereignty versus regional order.

One-sentence summary
The Roosevelt Corollary transformed the Monroe Doctrine from a warning to European powers into a justification for U.S. intervention in Latin America — a major turning point that cemented U.S. dominance in the hemisphere and left a contested legacy still relevant today.

Because Theodore Roosevelt National Park is divided into two distinct sections (the **South Unit** near Medora and the **North Unit** near Watford City), the best nearby stops depend on which unit you are visiting—or whether you're traveling between them. 

Here are the best things to see and do nearby, broken down by area:

---

### 1. In and Around Medora (South Unit Gateway)
If you base yourself near the South Unit, you’ll be in **Medora**, a historic, walkable frontier town packed with Old West charm.

* **Château de Mòres State Historic Site:** The 26-room summer home built in 1883 by the French nobleman Marquis de Mòres (who founded Medora and named it after his wife). The mansion contains original furnishings, and the nearby interpretive center explores his cattle ranching empire.
* **The Medora Musical & Pitchfork Fondue (Summer only):** Held in a dramatic outdoor amphitheater carved into the badlands, this high-energy musical runs nightly from early June through early September. Right before the show, enjoy steaks cooked on pitchforks overlooking the canyon.
* **Sully Creek State Park:** Located just a few miles south of Medora along the Little Missouri River, this is a quiet, scenic park popular for camping, horseback riding, and river paddling in spring/early summer.

---

### 2. North of the Park (North Unit & Williston Area)
The North Unit is wilder and more rugged than the South Unit. If you head up to Watford City or toward the Montana border, don’t miss:

* **Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site (~1 hour north of North Unit):** Situated on the North Dakota/Montana border, Fort Union was the most important fur trading post on the Upper Missouri River from 1828 to 1867. The reconstructed fort looks just as it did in the 1800s, with fantastic living history exhibits.
* **Fort Buford State Historic Site & Confluence Center:** Located just down the road from Fort Union, this is where the famous Lakota leader **Sitting Bull surrendered** in 1881. Nearby, the Missouri-Yellowstone Confluence Interpretive Center details Lewis and Clark’s expedition through the area.
* **Little Missouri State Park (~45 mins east of Watford City):** One of North Dakota’s most rugged, quiet parks. It features dramatic badlands ravines and over 45 miles of trails primarily used by hikers and horseback riders.

---

### 3. Outdoor Adventure Between the Units
* **The Maah Daah Hey Trail:** A world-renowned 144-mile non-motorized singletrack trail that winds through the Little Missouri National Grassland and connects both units of the national park. You don’t have to do the whole thing—short day hikes or mountain bike rides from various trailheads provide solitude and untamed badlands views.
* **Elkhorn Ranch Unit:** While technically part of the national park, this unit sits remote and isolated about halfway between the North and South Units down gravel roads. It marks the site of Roosevelt’s "home ranch," where he went to grieve and heal after the deaths of his wife and mother. Only foundation stones remain, but the peacefulness and wind rustling through the cottonwoods make it a reverent, quiet stop.

---

### 4. Road Trip Worthy Detours (Within 1 to 1.5 Hours)
* **The Enchanted Highway (1 hour east on I-94):** Stretching 32 miles from Gladstone south to Regent, this rural paved highway features the world’s largest scrap metal sculptures—including massive geese in flight, giant grasshoppers, and a towering metal family. It’s an iconic American roadside attraction.
* **Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson, 40 mins east on I-94):** Located at the Dickinson Museum Center, this museum holds the largest display of real dinosaur fossils on exhibit in North Dakota, including a complete Triceratops skull and tyrannosaur specimens found in the region.
* **Makoshika State Park (Glendive, MT – 1 hour west on I-94):** Montana’s largest state park features badlands topography that rivals TRNP, plus scenic drives, disc golf, and fossil trails (dinosaur remains like T-Rex and Triceratops have been uncovered here).

Medora, North Dakota, is a vibrant Old West town tucked against the rugged backdrop of the North Dakota Badlands. Despite its small permanent population, it is packed with history, outdoor adventure, and classic western charm. 

### 1. Explore Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
Medora serves as the gateway to the South Unit of the park, where Theodore Roosevelt ranched in the 1880s:
* **Wildlife Watching:** Drive the 36-mile Scenic Loop to spot free-roaming bison herds, wild feral horses, pronghorn, and massive prairie dog towns.
* **Maltese Cross Cabin:** Located right behind the South Unit Visitor Center, this preserved cabin is the original home TR lived in during his ranching days.
* **Scenic Hikes:** Take short, rewarding hikes like **Wind Canyon Trail** (stunning panoramic views of the Little Missouri River at sunset) and **Boicourt Overlook**, or trek longer paths like the **Petrified Forest Trail**.

### 2. See the Medora Musical & Eat Pitchfork Steak Fondue
A summertime staple, these two paired events offer the quintessential Medora experience:
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue:** Before the show, head up to the Tjaden Terrace for an authentic Western cookout where 12-ounce steaks are loaded onto pitchforks and deep-fried in large vats of oil, served buffet-style with Badlands views.
* **The Medora Musical:** Held nightly throughout the summer at the open-air Burning Hills Amphitheatre, this Broadway-style variety show features singing, dancing, live horses, patriotic numbers, and an Old West history lesson with badlands bluffs as the backdrop.

### 3. Visit the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
Set right into the Badlands landscape near Medora, this world-class institution explores TR’s life, conservation legacy, and the formative years he spent in North Dakota. Designed with striking eco-conscious architecture, it features immersive, hands-on exhibits, expansive views, and outdoor gathering spaces.

### 4. Tour the Chateau de Mòres State Historic Site
Medora was founded in 1883 by a flamboyant French nobleman, the Marquis de Mòres, who named the town after his wife, Medora von Hoffman. 
* **The Chateau:** A 26-room, two-story summer hunting lodge that still houses original furnishings and personal effects.
* **Packing Plant Ruins (Chimney Park):** A short walk away, you can see the surviving brick chimney from the Marquis’s ambitious but ill-fated refrigerated meatpacking venture.

### 5. Stroll Downtown Medora & the Cowboy Hall of Fame
* **Downtown Boardwalks:** Stroll the wooden sidewalks filled with boutique gift shops, ice cream parlors, and saloons. Stop into the historic **Rough Riders Hotel** for dinner or to view its extensive collection of Theodore Roosevelt books and memorabilia.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** A 15,000-square-foot interpretive center celebrating Western heritage, honoring the state's ranching, Native American, and rodeo history.
* **Harold Schafer Heritage Center:** Celebrates the philanthropist who helped restore and revitalize Medora into the historic destination it is today.

### 6. Play Bully Pulpit Golf Course
Ranked among the top public golf courses in the United States, Bully Pulpit winds through meadows, woodlands, and the rugged terrain of the Badlands. The dramatic stretch of back-nine holes—elevated tees looking over cliffs and ravines—offers unforgettable views.

### 7. Hike or Bike the Maah Daah Hey Trail
The legendary **Maah Daah Hey Trail** spans over 140 miles through the Badlands, connecting the South and North Units of Theodore Roosevelt National Park. Medora serves as a prime staging ground for mountain bikers, trail runners, and backpackers looking to tackle day sections or multi-day excursions.

### 8. Family Fun at Point to Point Park
If traveling with kids, Point to Point Park (located near downtown) offers:
* The **Manitou Zipline**, a dual zipline offering aerial views of the town.
* An 18-hole Badlands-themed mini-golf course.
* A public swimming pool and splash pad.

---

### Tips for Visiting:
* **Seasonality:** Peak season runs from **Memorial Day through Labor Day**, when the Medora Musical, outdoor attractions, and most shops are fully open. 
* **Shoulder Season:** Fall is quieter, cooler, and excellent for wildlife viewing and hiking without the summer crowds, though some town-based attractions operate on reduced schedules.

Here is a curated 3-day road trip itinerary covering the most iconic scenery, history, and roadside quirks of western North Dakota. 

---

### **Trip Overview**
* **Starting / Ending Hubs:** Bismarck (nearest commercial airport) or Dickinson
* **Route:** Bismarck/Dickinson → The Enchanted Highway → Medora (TRNP South Unit) → Watford City (TRNP North Unit) → Williston / Lake Sakakawea
* **Best Time to Visit:** June through September (when the *Medora Musical* runs and all park roads and facilities are fully open)

---

### **Day 1: Giant Roadside Sculptures & Historic Medora**

**Morning: The Enchanted Highway & Dickinson**
* **The Enchanted Highway:** Heading west along I-94, take exit 72 at Gladstone to drive south toward Regent. This 32-mile paved stretch features massive scrap-metal sculptures designed by local artist Gary Greff. Highlights include *Geese in Flight* (officially the world's largest scrap-metal sculpture), *Deer Crossing*, and *Tin Family*.
* **Dickinson:** Stop for lunch and visit the **Badlands Dinosaur Museum** (part of the Dickinson Museum Center), home to an impressive collection of real dinosaur fossils and full-scale skeletons discovered in the region.

**Afternoon: Welcome to the Badlands & Medora**
* **Painted Canyon Visitor Center:** Located directly off I-94 before Medora, this rest stop offers your first breathtaking panoramic overlook of the multicolored North Dakota Badlands.
* **Explore Medora:** Check in to your accommodations (the historic Rough Riders Hotel is a local staple). Medora is an authentic, preserved 1880s Western town.
* **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site:** Tour the 26-room summer residence built in 1883 by the eccentric French nobleman, the Marquis de Mores, who founded Medora and attempted to revolutionize the meat-packing industry.

**Evening: Western Classics**
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue & Medora Musical:** If traveling between June and early September, this is an absolute North Dakota staple. Enjoy ribeyes cooked on pitchforks over open vats of oil, followed by an energetic outdoor musical revue staged in the Burning Hills Amphitheatre overlooking the badlands.

---

### **Day 2: Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)**

**Morning: South Unit Scenic Loop**
* **Maltese Cross Cabin:** Located right behind the South Unit Visitor Center in Medora, this restored cabin is where a young Theodore Roosevelt lived during his early ranching days in the Dakota Territory.
* **South Unit Scenic Drive:** Drive the paved scenic loop winding through rugged coulees and buttes. 
  * Keep an eye out for free-roaming **bison herds, feral horses, and bighorn sheep**.
  * Stop at one of the massive **Prairie Dog Towns** right along the road.

**Afternoon: Iconic Hikes & Vistas**
* **Wind Canyon Trail:** A quick, easy 0.4-mile loop leading to wind-sculpted cliff edges with magnificent vistas over the Little Missouri River.
* **Boicourt Overlook:** One of the highest points in the South Unit, offering sweeping 360-degree views of the canyon breaks.
* **Buck Hill:** Take the short, steep spur trail to the park’s highest accessible point.

**Late Afternoon/Evening: Drive to Watford City**
* Drive north along **US-85** (about 1–1.5 hours) toward Watford City. Along the way, you’ll cross the historic **Long X Bridge** over the Little Missouri River.
* **Overnight in Watford City:** A lively prairie town that has evolved with the energy industry. Grab dinner and local craft beer at **Stonehome Brewing Company**.

---

### **Day 3: TRNP (North Unit) & Historic Frontier Posts**

**Morning: Theodore Roosevelt National Park (North Unit)**
* The North Unit is less visited than the South Unit, but many consider it far more rugged, dramatic, and wild.
* **North Unit Scenic Drive:** A 14-mile out-and-back route along the rim and floor of the Little Missouri River Valley.
* **Riverbend Overlook:** The quintessential photo spot of North Dakota—a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) perched high on a cliff above a dramatic oxbow bend in the river.
* **Cannonball Concretions:** Check out the bizarre, spherical rock formations naturally eroded out of the badlands sediment.
* **Oxbow Overlook:** The end of the scenic drive, offering sheer drops down into the winding river bottom.

**Afternoon: Choose Your Route Back**

* **Option A (Fur-Trade & Lewis & Clark History):** 
  * Drive 45 minutes northwest to **Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site** near the Montana border. Between 1828 and 1867, this reconstructed palisaded fort was the most important fur-trade post on the Upper Missouri, where Assiniboine, Crow, and other tribes traded buffalo robes for goods.
  * Nearby, visit the **Missouri-Yellowstone Confluence Interpretive Center**, where Lewis and Clark camped in 1805.
* **Option B (Scenic Lakes & Gorges):** 
  * Head east along Highway 200 through the **Killdeer Mountains** and across the **Four Bears Memorial Bridge** spanning Lake Sakakawea, returning toward Bismarck.

---

### **Essential Road Trip Tips**
1. **Wildlife Distance:** North Dakota bison are completely wild. Maintain at least a 25-yard distance (stay in or very close to your car if they are near the road).
2. **Cell Service:** Coverage can be sparse inside the national park canyons and remote stretches of Highway 85; download your offline maps in advance.
3. **Park Passes:** Your standard National Park Pass (America the Beautiful) covers both the South and North Units of Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

The drive from Mount Rushmore (Keystone, SD) to Theodore Roosevelt National Park (typically entering at the South Unit in Medora, ND) is roughly **4 to 4.5 hours (around 240–260 miles)** via the most direct route along **US-85 North**. 

While much of the drive crosses wide-open northern high plains, there are several worthwhile stops—ranging from 15-minute photo ops right off the highway to legendary detours.

Here are the best stops organized from south to north:

---

### 1. Northern Black Hills (SD)
Before you hit the open prairie, you’ll cut through the northern edge of the Black Hills:

* **Deadwood, SD:** Famous for its rough-and-tumble Gold Rush history. Walk the historic Main Street, visit the graves of Wild Bill Hickok and Calamity Jane at Mount Moriah Cemetery, or grab lunch at an Old West saloon.
* **Spearfish Canyon Scenic Byway (Hwy 14A):** If you have an extra hour, take this byway between Lead and Spearfish. The towering limestone canyon walls are stunning, and you can take quick, easy walks to **Bridal Veil Falls**, **Roughlock Falls**, or **Spearfish Falls**.

---

### 2. The Bucket-List Detour: Devils Tower National Monument (WY)
* **The Detour:** Heading west into Wyoming before turning north adds about **1.5 to 2 hours** of driving, but it’s the most iconic attraction between the two parks.
* **What to do:** Walk the paved 1.3-mile **Tower Trail** right around the base of the massive volcanic monolith, watch rock climbers tackle the sheer columns, and check out the resident prairie dog towns near the entrance.

---

### 3. Along US-85 North (SD into ND)
Once you leave Spearfish/Belle Fourche heading north, towns become few and far between:

* **Center of the Nation Monument (Belle Fourche, SD):** Belle Fourche is the official geographic center of the 50 United States (designated after Alaska and Hawaii joined). Stop by the Tri-State Museum to see the giant 21-foot granite compass rose monument for a quick road-trip photo.
* **Slim Buttes / The Castles (Custer National Forest, SD):** North of Belle Fourche along SD-20 / US-85 near Reva, the flat prairie unexpectedly gives way to dramatic white-and-green sandstone cliffs and bluffs. It's also the historic site of the 1876 Battle of Slim Buttes.
* **White Butte (Near Bowman/Amidon, ND):** If you're a high-pointer, the highest natural elevation in North Dakota (3,506 ft) is located just east of US-85 on private land with public foot access. It’s a quiet, scenic prairie hike of about 1.5 miles round-trip.

---

### 4. Roadside Art Detour: The Enchanted Highway (ND)
* **The Detour:** As you reach I-94 in North Dakota, driving about 30 minutes east brings you to Regent, ND.
* **What to see:** A 32-mile stretch of country road lined with giant scrap-metal folk sculptures, including *"Geese in Flight"* (recognized as one of the world's largest scrap-metal sculptures), *"Deer Crossing"*, and *"Grasshoppers in the Field"*.

---

### 5. Gateway to TRNP: Medora, ND
Right at the entrance to Theodore Roosevelt National Park's South Unit:

* **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site:** The preserved 26-room summer home of the flamboyant French nobleman who founded Medora in 1883.
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue & Medora Musical (Summer only):** Steaks cooked on actual pitchforks overlooking the Badlands amphitheater, followed by the long-running Western variety show.

---

### Practical Travel Tips:
* **Gas up in Belle Fourche or Bowman:** The stretch of US-85 between Belle Fourche, SD, and Bowman, ND (roughly 85 miles) is very remote with minimal cell service and few places to buy fuel.
* **Wildlife:** Keep an eye out for pronghorn antelope along the fence lines throughout the plains portion of US-85.

Traveling across North Dakota on Interstate 94 takes you through shifting landscapes—from the flat, fertile Red River Valley in the east to the rugged Badlands in the west. 

Here are the best stops along I-94, organized from **East to West** (Fargo to the Montana border):

---

### 1. Fargo & West Fargo (Mile Markers 348–343)
* **The Woodchipper at the Visitors Center:** Stop by the Fargo-Moorhead Visitors Center (Exit 348) to see the original movie prop woodchipper from the Coen brothers' film *Fargo*, complete with faux-fur hats for photos.
* **Fargo Air Museum:** Located near the interstate, featuring flyable vintage aircraft from WWII through the modern era.
* **Bonanzaville, USA (West Fargo):** A 12-acre pioneer village with dozens of historic buildings, vintage automobiles, tractors, and frontier artifacts.

---

### 2. Valley City (Mile Marker 292)
* **Hi-Line Railroad Bridge:** Valley City is known as the "City of Bridges." The highlight is this towering single-track trestle built in 1908, measuring 3,860 feet long and standing 162 feet above the Sheyenne River.
* **Medicine Wheel Park:** Features a modern recreation of Native American stone medicine wheels, a solar calendar, and scenic views of the Sheyenne River Valley.

---

### 3. Jamestown (Mile Marker 258)
* **The World’s Largest Buffalo ("Dakota Thunder"):** A 26-foot-tall, 60-ton concrete bison monument overlooking the prairie.
* **National Buffalo Museum & Live Herd:** Located right by the giant buffalo, this museum explores the cultural and ecological history of the American bison, with viewing pastures for a live herd.
* **Frontier Village:** A replica 1880s prairie town that includes Louis L’Amour’s original writer’s shack (the famous Western author was born in Jamestown).

---

### 4. Steele (Mile Marker 200)
* **The World’s Largest Sandhill Crane ("Sandy"):** Steele is located in a prime migratory bird corridor. Just off the highway, you can grab a quick photo with "Sandy," a 40-foot-tall steel-and-wire sculpture.

---

### 5. Bismarck–Mandan (Mile Markers 159–153)
* **North Dakota Heritage Center & State Museum:** Located on the State Capitol grounds in Bismarck, this world-class (and free) museum covers everything from T. rex skeletons and Native American history to space suits.
* **North Dakota State Capitol:** Known as the "Skyscraper on the Prairie," this 19-story Art Deco tower is one of only a handful of tower-style capitols in the country.
* **Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park (Mandan):** Located just south across the Missouri River, this park features the reconstructed Custer House and the reconstructed On-A-Slant Mandan Indian Village with authentic earth lodges.

---

### 6. New Salem (Mile Marker 127)
* **Salem Sue (The World's Largest Holstein Cow):** Perched high on School Hill overlooking I-94, this 38-foot-high, 12,000-pound fiberglass dairy cow honors the area's dairy industry and offers sweeping 360-degree views of the prairie.

---

### 7. Richardton (Mile Marker 84)
* **Assumption Abbey:** A striking Bavarian-Romanesque monastery founded by Benedictine monks in the late 1800s. Its twin spires dominate the prairie skyline, and self-guided tours of the cathedral-like church are welcome.

---

### 8. Gladstone / Regent (Mile Marker 72)
* **The Enchanted Highway:** Right at Exit 72 sits *"Geese in Flight,"* recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world's largest scrap-metal sculpture. If you have an hour to spare, the full 32-mile paved detour south to Regent features gigantic scrap-metal sculptures of deer, grasshoppers, pheasants, and fishermen.

---

### 9. Dickinson (Mile Markers 61–59)
* **Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson Museum Center):** Home to one of the largest displays of real dinosaur fossils in the northern plains, including complete skeletons found locally in the Hell Creek Formation.
* **Ukrainian Cultural Institute:** Celebrates the rich heritage of the Ukrainian immigrants who settled in western North Dakota, featuring traditional folk art, textiles, and intricately decorated *pysanky* (Ukrainian Easter eggs).

---

### 10. Medora & Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Mile Markers 32–23)
* **Painted Canyon Visitor Center (Mile Marker 32):** Even if you don't enter the town of Medora, this rest stop is directly accessible from I-94 and delivers an immediate panoramic overlook of the multicolored Badlands.
* **Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit):** Famous for colorful layered canyons, free-roaming wild horses, bison herds, and prairie dog towns. Drive the 36-mile scenic loop through the park.
* **Historic Town of Medora:** A charming Old West-style town featuring:
  * **The Medora Musical:** A western musical revue performed in an open-air amphitheater set against the canyon walls (summer season).
  * **Chateau de Mores:** The 26-room summer home of the French nobleman Marquis de Mores, who founded Medora in 1883.

The North Dakota Badlands—anchored by **Theodore Roosevelt National Park** and the historic western town of **Medora**—are a fantastic destination for families. The landscape feels like a giant outdoor playground, packed with wildlife, easy trails, and Old West charm.

Here are some of the most fun things to do with kids in the area:

---

### 1. Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South & North Units)

* **Visit a Prairie Dog Town:** This is usually a kid favorite. Along the South Unit’s scenic drive, you'll encounter large prairie dog “towns.” Kids can watch them pop out of their burrows, chirp, and do their signature “jump-yips.” 
* **Go on a "Safari" for Bison and Wild Horses:** Theodore Roosevelt National Park is home to hundreds of wild bison and feral horses, as well as elk, pronghorn, and bighorn sheep. Bring a pair of binoculars for the kids to spot them from the safety of your car or an overlook. *(Always remind kids to keep a safe distance—at least 25 yards from horses and 100 yards from bison!)*
* **Earn a Junior Ranger Badge:** Stop by the South Unit Visitor Center (Medora) or North Unit Visitor Center (Watford City). Pick up a free Junior Ranger activity booklet. Once completed, park rangers will swear the kids in and award them an official wooden badge.
* **Hike Kid-Friendly Trails:**
  * **Wind Canyon Trail (South Unit):** A short, 0.4-mile loop with wind-sculpted rock walls and breathtaking panoramic views over the Little Missouri River.
  * **Boicourt Overlook Trail (South Unit):** A flat, paved 0.2-mile walk with one of the most colorful views in the Badlands—great for toddlers and strollers.
  * **Painted Canyon Nature Trail (Off I-94):** Located right at the rest stop/visitor center; kids can gaze into the colorful canyon and do an easy rim walk.
* **Explore TR's Maltese Cross Cabin:** Located right behind the South Unit Visitor Center, this preserved 1880s log cabin shows kids how Theodore Roosevelt lived when he was a rancher in the Dakota Territory.

---

### 2. Fun in the Historic Town of Medora

Medora sits right at the entrance to the South Unit and feels like stepping onto an Old West movie set:

* **Medora Children’s Park:** Located on the edge of town, this isn't just an ordinary playground. It’s a massive, multi-level wooden western fort complete with towers, tunnels, bridges, a pretend stagecoach, and a train engine. It’s free and one of the best town playgrounds in the state.
* **The Medora Musical (Summer only):** An outdoor, variety-style Broadway musical held in the Burning Hills Amphitheater nestled right in a Badlands canyon. It features live horses on stage, western songs, country humor, and fireworks at the finale.
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue:** Held right next to the amphitheater before the musical. Chefs plunge 12-ounce steaks on pitchforks into giant cauldrons of boiling oil. It’s fun theatre for the kids, and they serve hot dogs and family-friendly sides too.
* **Little Bully Pulpit Mini Golf:** An 18-hole miniature golf course right downtown Medora that features western themes and hazards.
* **Treat Stops:** Grab homemade fudge, giant scoops of ice cream, or old-fashioned sodas at the Medora Fudge & Ice Cream Depot.

---

### 3. Outdoor Adventures & Hands-on History

* **Horseback Trail Rides:** Several stables around Medora (such as Medora Riding Stables) offer guided trail rides for kids and beginners through the canyon draws and over the buttes. 
* **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site:** A 26-room hunting lodge built in 1883 by the French nobleman Marquis de Mores. Kids love touring the preserved rooms packed with antique weapons, vintage clothes, and outdoor interpretive trails.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** An interactive museum in Medora showcasing real ranching, rodeo, and Native American gear, saddles, and outfits. 
* **Epic Stargazing:** The Badlands have some of the darkest night skies in the country. On clear summer nights, bring a blanket and look for the Milky Way, shooting stars, and occasionally even the Northern Lights.

---

### Tips for Visiting with Kids:
* **Footwear:** Badlands clay can be slippery when dry and like wet cement after rain. Sturdy sneakers or hiking shoes are much better than flip-flops or sandals.
* **Sun & Bugs:** The Badlands get hot in the summer with very little shade. Pack wide-brim hats, sunscreen, and plenty of extra water for every hike.
* **Cactus & Critters:** Remind little ones to stay on established trails—prickly pear cactus grows low to the ground, and prairie rattlesnakes live in the grasses.

Here are the best museums in North Dakota, categorized by interest:

---

### **The Flagship Museum**
* **North Dakota Heritage Center & State Museum (Bismarck)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Located on the State Capitol grounds, this is the premier museum in the state and offers **free admission**. 
  * **Highlights:** Four massive permanent galleries covering geological history (including incredible dinosaur and mosasaur skeletons), Native American culture, early settlement and military history, and modern North Dakota. The stunning glass "Northern Lights Atrium" is an architectural highlight.

---

### **History, Frontier & Cultural Heritage**
* **Bonanzaville, USA (West Fargo)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Operated by the Cass County Historical Society, this 12-acre pioneer village features over 40 historic buildings moved from across the region.
  * **Highlights:** An authentic 1880s prairie town with a saloon, jail, schoolhouses, a church, medical museums, vintage automobiles, and aircraft exhibits.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame (Medora)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Located in the scenic gateway town to Theodore Roosevelt National Park, it honors the history of rodeo, ranching, and Native American cultures in the western plains.
  * **Highlights:** Engaging exhibits detailing the life of Plains cowboys, Native cultures, horse culture, and legendary regional figures.
* **National Buffalo Museum (Jamestown)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Dedicated entirely to the cultural, historical, and ecological significance of the American bison.
  * **Highlights:** Extensive exhibits tracing the rise, near-extinction, and recovery of bison herds. Right outside, you'll find a live bison herd and the famous 26-foot-tall "World's Largest Buffalo" monument.
* **Scandinavian Heritage Park (Minot)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Celebrates the heritage of immigrants from Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Iceland.
  * **Highlights:** Outdoor replicas and authentic historic structures, most notably a full-scale replica of the famous **Gol Stave Church**, a Finnish sauna, and a giant Swedish Dala horse.

---

### **Aviation & Military**
* **Fargo Air Museum (Fargo)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Located right next to Hector International Airport, it’s one of the top aviation collections in the Upper Midwest.
  * **Highlights:** A rotating collection of historic aircraft ranging from World War II fighters (like P-51 Mustangs) to modern jets and helicopters—many of which are maintained in fully operational, flight-ready condition.
* **Dakota Territory Air Museum (Minot)**
  * **Why it’s great:** A must-see for WWII buffs, featuring one of the most respected vintage warbird restorations and military collections in the country.
  * **Highlights:** Rare WWII fighters, civilian planes, and artifacts documenting Minot’s deep ties to military aviation.

---

### **Art & Science**
* **Plains Art Museum (Fargo)**
  * **Why it’s great:** The largest and only accredited art museum in North Dakota, housed in a beautifully renovated historic brick warehouse in downtown Fargo.
  * **Highlights:** A collection of over 4,000 works with a heavy emphasis on contemporary regional artists, Native American art, and traditional printmaking.
* **Pioneer Trails Regional Museum (Bowman)**
  * **Why it’s great:** Tucked away in southwestern North Dakota near the fossil-rich Hell Creek Formation, this museum punches far above its weight in paleontology and archaeology.
  * **Highlights:** An active field station and paleontology lab where visitors can view real dinosaur and ancient mammal fossils found directly in the surrounding Badlands.

---

### **Historic Living Sites (Honorable Mention)**
* **Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site (Stanton):** Features an excellent museum and rebuilt earthlodge showcasing the rich agricultural trading empire of the Northern Plains tribes (Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara).

* **Location:** Chicago, Illinois

The Obama administration transitioned to a new "digital-first" model with the National Archives: NARA administers his official records and classified materials digitally, while the physical campus (which includes a museum, public park, and a branch of the Chicago Public Library) is independently owned and operated by the Obama Foundation.

### 3. Newest Traditional NARA-Operated Facility: **George W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum** (Opened May 2013)
* **Location:** Dallas, Texas (Southern Methodist University campus)
* **Details:** If looking strictly at the federal network of 15+ official presidential library buildings constructed and turned over to NARA to house both physical archival research facilities and public museums, George W. While all 15 official National Archives (NARA) presidential libraries offer rich historical archives, some stand out far above the rest for their interactive exhibits, historic artifacts, stunning architecture, and overall visitor experience. 

Here are the top presidential libraries most widely considered worth traveling to see:

---

### 1. The Blockbuster Experiences

#### **Ronald Reagan Presidential Library** *(Simi Valley, California)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** Often ranked the #1 visitor experience. Perched on a scenic mountaintop overlooking the Simi Valley and the Pacific Ocean, it feels more like a major historical theme park than a traditional library.
* **Standout features:**
  * **Air Force One Pavilion:** You can walk through the actual Boeing 707 used by Reagan (and six other presidents), along with a Marine One helicopter.
  * A full-scale replica of the Oval Office and an authentic, reassembled Irish pub from Reagan’s ancestral hometown in Ballyporeen, Ireland.
  * An actual section of the Berlin Wall outdoors against sweeping canyon views.

#### **Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum** *(Springfield, Illinois)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** While operated by the state of Illinois rather than the federal government, this is universally regarded as one of the most engaging presidential museums in the nation. 
* **Standout features:**
  * Highly immersive, theatrical storytelling using life-size dioramas, special-effects theater ("Ghosts of the Library"), and interactive holofilm technology.
  * You can combine it with a visit to the Lincoln Home National Historic Site and Lincoln’s Tomb, both located nearby in Springfield.

---

### 2. The Great Historic Estates

#### **Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum** *(Hyde Park, New York)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** FDR essentially invented the modern presidential library. Designed by Roosevelt himself in Dutch colonial revival style, it covers the two defining crises of the 20th century: the Great Depression and World War II.
* **Standout features:**
  * Located on his historic estate, **Springwood**, overlooking the Hudson River.
  * Exhibits detail the New Deal, his fireside chats, and his modified 1936 Ford convertible equipped with hand controls.
  * You can also tour Eleanor Roosevelt’s retreat, **Val-Kill**, and Top Cottage on the same trip.

#### **Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum** *(Independence, Missouri)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** The Truman Library recently underwent a massive, acclaimed $30+ million modernization. It is widely praised by historians for its unvarnished look at some of the most momentous decisions in modern history.

Several prominent historic sites throughout the United States are dedicated to or closely associated with Theodore Roosevelt. Most are managed by the National Park Service:

### 1. Sagamore Hill National Historic Site (Oyster Bay, New York)
* **Significance:** Often called Roosevelt’s **"Summer White House,"** this Victorian mansion served as his primary home from 1885 until his death in 1919. 
* **Key Features:** During his presidency, Roosevelt hosted world leaders, treated with foreign dignitaries (including negotiations leading to the Treaty of Portsmouth), and spent summers with his family here. The house retains original furnishings, taxidermy, library books, and hunting trophies. The property also features nature trails and the Theodore Roosevelt Museum at the Old Orchard home.

### 2. Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site (New York City, New York)
* **Significance:** Located in Manhattan’s Flatiron District (28 East 20th Street), this reconstructed four-story brownstone stands on the site where "Teedie" was born in 1858 and lived until he was 14.
* **Key Features:** Period rooms recreate the Roosevelts' wealthy lifestyle, the outdoor gymnasium his father built to help young Theodore overcome severe asthma, and a museum containing family artifacts and Rough Rider memorabilia.

### 3. Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site (Buffalo, New York)
* **Significance:** Known historically as the **Ansley Wilcox House**, this is the site where Theodore Roosevelt took the oath of office as the 26th President on September 14, 1901, following the assassination of President William McKinley at the Pan-American Exposition.
* **Key Features:** Visitors can tour the library where Roosevelt was sworn in and view exhibits covering McKinley’s assassination, the transition of power, and Roosevelt’s progressive agenda.

### 4. Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Medora, North Dakota)
* **Significance:** Roosevelt first arrived in the Dakota Badlands in 1883 to hunt bison and cope with grief after the deaths of his wife, Alice, and mother, Martha, on the same day in 1884. His years living and ranching in the West profoundly shaped his character and fueled his passion for conservation.
* **Key Features:** 
  * **Maltese Cross Cabin:** Roosevelt’s first cabin, preserved and relocated to the South Unit Visitor Center in Medora.
  * **Elkhorn Ranch Site:** Roosevelt’s beloved "home ranch" along the Little Missouri River, which he described as his favorite place in the Badlands.

### 5. Theodore Roosevelt Island (Washington, D.C.)
* **Significance:** An 88.5-acre island in the Potomac River preserved as a "living memorial" to Roosevelt's conservation legacy. 
* **Key Features:** Designed by the famous landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted Jr., the island features nature trails, wooded wetlands, and a memorial plaza centered around a 17-foot bronze statue of Roosevelt accompanied by four large granite monoliths carved with his famous quotes on nature, youth, and the state.

### 6. Pine Knot (Keene / Albemarle County, Virginia)
* **Significance:** A modest, rustic woodland cabin purchased by Edith Roosevelt in 1905 to serve as a quiet weekend retreat away from the pressures of Washington.
* **Key Features:** Roosevelt used Pine Knot for birdwatching, hiking, hunting, and escaping political life. It is preserved today by the Edith and Theodore Roosevelt Pine Knot Foundation.

---

* **Mount Rushmore National Memorial (Keystone, South Dakota):** Roosevelt's face is carved into the granite alongside George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Abraham Lincoln to represent the nation’s growth and the progressive era.
* **The White House (Washington, D.C.):** In 1901, Roosevelt officially made "The White House" the mansion's formal name (replacing "Executive Mansion") and oversaw the 1902 renovation that built the original West Wing.
* **Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library (Medora, North Dakota):** Established near the Badlands to house his personal papers, digital archives, and exhibits on his conservation legacy.
* **Youngs Memorial Cemetery (Oyster Bay, New York):** The peaceful hilltop cemetery where Theodore and Edith Roosevelt are buried, located near Sagamore Hill.

The **Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library** in **Medora, North Dakota** is widely considered **well worth visiting**—particularly if you pair it with a broader trip to Theodore Roosevelt National Park and the surrounding Badlands. 

The site features several unique elements, along with key travel considerations to help plan a visit:

---

### What Makes It Worth the Trip

* **World-Class Architecture and Setting:**  
  Designed by the internationally acclaimed architecture firm **Snøhetta**, the library is built seamlessly into a 93-acre butte overlooking the North Dakota Badlands. The building features walkable, planted green rooftops and outdoor boardwalk trails that connect indoor galleries directly into the rugged prairie landscape. 

* **Emotional and Historical Resonance:**  
  Unlike presidential libraries located in presidential birthplaces or suburban research parks, this facility is located in the exact landscape that Theodore Roosevelt credited with forging his identity. Following the sudden deaths of his wife and mother on the same day in 1884, Roosevelt retreated to the Badlands to grieve, ranch, and rebuild his stamina. As he later said, *“I never would have been President if it had not been for my experiences in North Dakota.”* Experiencing his conservation legacy while overlooking the Badlands creates a rare sense of place.

* **Modern, Immersive Exhibition Design:**  
  Moving away from static rows of glass display cases, the library uses interactive exhibits, narrative storytelling galleries, and immersive digital media. It traces his full arc—from a sickly child in New York to a Western rancher, Rough Rider, progressive reformer, and global explorer. Most visitors plan about 3 to 4 hours to take in the main galleries, theater, and boardwalk.

* **Synergy with Surrounding Attractions:**  
  The library sits at the doorstep of the **South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park**, making Medora an exceptional hub. Within minutes, you can spot bison and wild horses on the park’s scenic loop, visit the historic Chateau de Mores, or explore the Old West charm of downtown Medora.

---

### Things to Keep in Mind Before Going

* **Remote Location:**  
  Medora is in western North Dakota, roughly a 2-hour drive from Bismarck and about 4 to 5 hours from regional hubs like Billings, Montana, or Rapid City, South Dakota. Most visitors will need to plan a dedicated road trip or connect via regional flights into Bismarck or Dickinson.
* **Heavy Seasonality in Medora:**  
  While the library is designed as a year-round destination, **Medora itself is a highly seasonal town**. Between Memorial Day and Labor Day, town amenities—restaurants, historic shops, and the famous outdoor *Medora Musical*—are in full swing. If you visit in late fall, winter, or early spring, western North Dakota weather can be harsh, and many local dining and lodging options operate on sharply reduced hours or close entirely.
* **Timed-Entry Reservations:**  
  Because of steady interest and capacity limits within the galleries, reserving **advance timed-entry tickets** online before your arrival is strongly recommended.

---

### The Verdict
If you are a fan of presidential history, conservation, or innovative architecture, the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library is an exceptional cultural destination. For the best overall experience, visit between **June and late September**, allowing enough time to hike or drive through Theodore Roosevelt National Park and spend an evening in Medora.

**The Square Deal** was President Theodore Roosevelt’s domestic policy platform, introduced during his presidency (1901–1909). Rooted in the Progressive Era, the policy aimed to balance the competing interests of labor, business, and the public. Roosevelt believed that the federal government should act as a neutral arbitrator to ensure that average citizens received a fair opportunity—a "square deal"—while preventing wealthy monopolies or radical labor unions from abusing their power.

The Square Deal is historically remembered by its **"Three Cs"**:
1. **Control of corporations**
2. **Consumer protection**
3. **Conservation of natural resources**

---

### 1. Control of Corporations
During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, massive trusts and monopolies dominated American industry, stifling competition and exploiting workers. Roosevelt did not believe all big businesses were inherently bad; instead, he distinguished between:
* **"Good trusts"**: Companies that provided efficient services and fair prices, which should be regulated.
* **"Bad trusts"**: Companies that abused their power to artificially inflate prices, crush competitors, or exploit workers, which needed to be broken up.

**Key Actions:**
* **Trust-Busting:** Roosevelt revitalized the long-dormant *Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890*. His administration filed over 40 antitrust suits, famously breaking up J.P. Morgan’s railroad monopoly, the **Northern Securities Company**, in 1904, as well as initiating cases against Standard Oil and the American Tobacco Company.
* **Railroad Regulation:** Unfair railroad rebates favored large conglomerates over small farmers and shippers. Roosevelt signed the **Elkins Act (1903)** and the **Hepburn Act (1906)**, which significantly empowered the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) to set maximum freight rates and curb predatory pricing.
* **Mediation of Labor Conflicts:** During the **1902 Anthracite Coal Strike**, winter approached with the nation facing a severe coal shortage. Instead of sending federal troops to break the strike on behalf of mine owners (as past presidents had done), Roosevelt brought union leaders and management to the White House to negotiate, threatening to nationalize the mines if they refused to compromise. This marked the first time the federal government intervened as an impartial mediator rather than a strikebreaker.

---

### 2. Consumer Protection
The rapid rise of industrial manufacturing led to poor safety standards, unsanitary conditions, and fraudulent labeling in everyday goods, particularly food and medicine. 

**Key Actions:**
* **Response to *The Jungle*:** In 1906, muckraking journalist Upton Sinclair published *The Jungle*, exposing the horrifying, unsanitary conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking facilities. Public outrage prompted Roosevelt to launch an investigation.
* **The Meat Inspection Act (1906):** Dictated strict sanitary standards for meat processing plants and mandated federal inspection of all meat crossing state lines.
* **The Pure Food and Drug Act (1906):** Halted the manufacture and sale of adulterated, toxic, or misbranded food and medicine, while requiring truthful ingredient labels (such as disclosing the presence of alcohol, cocaine, or morphine). This legislation laid the foundation for what eventually became the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

---

### 3. Conservation of Natural Resources
Roosevelt was an avid outdoorsman and saw the unrestricted exploitation of America's forests, minerals, and waterways by private corporations as a national crisis. Alongside his chief forester, **Gifford Pinchot**, Roosevelt championed a policy of "scientific management" and conservation—using resources efficiently and sustainably so future generations could benefit from them.

**Key Actions:**
* **Public Land Preservation:** Roosevelt used executive power to place roughly 230 million acres under federal protection. This included 150 national forests, 51 federal bird reserves, four national game preserves, and five national parks.
* **The Antiquities Act (1906):** Enabled the president to designate historic landmarks, structures, and objects of scientific interest as national monuments without needing congressional approval. Under this act, Roosevelt protected sites such as the Grand Canyon and Devils Tower.
* **Newlands Reclamation Act (1902):** Funded massive irrigation and dam projects across the arid American West, fostering sustainable agricultural development.

### Significance and Legacy
The Square Deal fundamentally transformed the role of the U.S. presidency and the federal government. Prior to Roosevelt, the government largely adhered to a *laissez-faire* (hands-off) approach, often intervening only to protect corporate property during strikes. 

Roosevelt redefined the federal government as a steward of the public interest, establishing the precedent that the state has an obligation to regulate big business, safeguard public health, and protect natural resources. His framework heavily influenced future domestic agendas, notably Woodrow Wilson's "New Freedom" and his distant cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt's "New Deal."
